The **Lockheed SR-71** "**Blackbird**" is a retired long-range, high-altitude, Mach3+ strategicreconnaissance aircraft that was developed and manufactured by the American aerospace company Lockheed Corporation.[[N 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-1) Its nicknames include "Blackbird" and "Habu".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrickmore199764-2)

The SR-71 was developed in the 1960s as a black project by Lockheed's Skunk Works division. American aerospace engineer Clarence "Kelly" Johnson was responsible for many of the SR-71's innovative concepts.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-3) Its shape was based on the Lockheed A-12, a pioneer in stealth technology with its reduced radar cross section, but the SR-71 was longer and heavier to carry more fuel and a crew of two in tandem cockpits. The SR-71 was revealed to the public in July 1964 and entered service in the United States Air Force (USAF) in January 1966.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-4)
During missions, the SR-71 operated at high speeds and altitudes (Mach 3.2 at 85,000 ft or 26,000 m), allowing it to evade or outrace threats.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-outran-5) If a surface-to-air missile launch was detected, the standard evasive action was to accelerate and outpace the missile.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-SR71_Blackbird_2006-6) Equipment for the plane's aerial reconnaissance missions included signals-intelligence sensors, side-looking airborne radar, and a camera.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-outran-5) On average, an SR-71 could fly just once per week because of the lengthy preparations needed. A total of 32 aircraft were built; 12 were lost in accidents, none to enemy action.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-Landis_p98-101-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-Pace_p126-7-8)

From 1968, reconnaissance missions were flown from Kadena AB, Okinawa, first over North Vietnam and Laos during the Vietnam War, and later over North Korea. From 1976, missions were flown from RAF Mildenhall, UK, along the Soviet Union's Baltic and Barents Sea coastlines. Missions were also flown over Cuba, Nicaragua, Libya, and to probe nuclear weapons installations in Israel and South Africa.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-:0-9) Unlike previous aircraft that were under the Central Intelligence Agency, SR-71 missions were flown overtly, with USAF markings, and never overflew the Warsaw Pact or China.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-10)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-:0-9)
In 1974, the SR-71 set the record for the quickest flight between London and New York at 1 hour, 54 minutes and 56 seconds.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-11) In 1976, it became the fastest airbreathing manned aircraft, previously held by its predecessor, the closely related Lockheed YF-12.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-landis_jenkins_p78-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-Pace_p159-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FAI_records-14)As of 2026, the Blackbird still holds both world records.

In 1989, the USAF retired the SR-71,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-:0-9) although several aircraft were briefly reactivated before their second retirement in 1998. NASA was the final operator of the Blackbird, using it as a research platform, until it was retired again in 1999.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-15) Since its retirement, the SR-71's role has been taken up by a combination of reconnaissance satellites and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). As of 2018, Lockheed Martin was developing a proposed UAV successor, the SR-72; however, as of 2026, the design remains a concept.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-US_pushes_hard-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-17)

Lockheed's previous reconnaissance aircraft was the relatively slow U-2, designed for the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). In late 1957, the CIA approached the defense contractor Lockheed to build an undetectable spy plane. The project, named Archangel, was led by Kelly Johnson, head of Lockheed's Skunk Works unit in Burbank, California. The work on project Archangel began in the second quarter of 1958, with aim of flying higher and faster than the U-2. Of 11 successive designs drafted in a span of 10 months, "A-10" was the front-runner, although its shape made it vulnerable to radar detection. After a meeting with the CIA in March 1959, the design was modified to reduce its radar cross-section by 90%. On 11 February 1960, the CIA approved a US$96 million (~$799 million in 2025) contract for Skunk Works to build a dozen A-12 spy planes. Three months later, the May 1960 downing of Francis Gary Powers's U-2 underscored the need for less vulnerable reconnaissance aircraft.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-18)

The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird was a two-seat twin-engine long-range supersonic strategic reconnaissance aircraft produced by Lockheed Corporation. The SR-71 was capable of flying at speeds over Mach 3.2 and at a height of 85,000 feet (25,900 Meter). The SR-71 was in duty from 1964 until 1989 and during a reactivation from 1993 until 1998. It was designed by the Lockheed Advanced Development Projects Devision aka the Lockheed Skunk Works.

The Blackbirds still hold many speed, altitude and distance records for a manned aircraft.

Source: https://simpleflying.com/fastest-aircraft-ever-built/
Title: What Is The Fastest Aircraft Ever Built?
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5
A Cessna 172 can typically cruise at around 140 mph (225 kph). Most commercial airliners fly fast enough at altitude that speed is measured in how close the aircraft's speed is to the speed of sound. A Boeing 777, for example, cruises at Mach 0.84, or 84% the speed of sound. Supersonic aircraft fly past Mach 1, the speed of sound, and the Concorde could fly past Mach 2. But even this is slow compared to the fastest military aircraft ever built.
The MiG-25 Foxbat is the fastest fighter jet to have ever been in regular service. Its top speed was typically limited to Mach 2.83; however, it could reach Mach 3.2 for a few minutes at a time if the pilots pushed it. The one aircraft that could beat it in speed is the legendary Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird, one of the most famous military aircraft of all time. It could maintain up to Mach 3.2 for extended periods of time, and even reach **Mach 3.3**in specific circumstances.

## The Records Held By The SR-71 Blackbird
The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird currently holds the record for the fastest sustained flight by a manned air-breathing aircraft, when it reached a speed of **Mach 3.3, or 2,193 mph (3,529.6 kph)** in 1976. Additionally, the SR-71 also holds the record for the highest altitude reached in sustained horizontal flight, when on the same day it reached **85,069 ft**.
The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird was able to complete a flight from the American West Coast to the Eastern Seaboard in one hour and seven minutes, and it flew from New York to London in less than two hours. For reference, the Concorde typically flew between the world's two most influential cities in three hours, while a subsonic airliner today takes between five and six hours to fly between the American coasts.
To date, no manned military aircraft has matched the speed and altitude capabilities of the SR-71. Even the famous MiG-25, which holds the absolute altitude record when it reached nearly 125,000 ft in a zoom climb, was limited to 78,740 ft in straight and level flight. The SR-71 was truly an invulnerable aircraft, proven by the fact that no SR-71 or SR-71 variant was ever shot down in combat.

## The Origin Of The Lockheed SR-71
Credit:Photo:NYC Russ I Shutterstock
In the 1950s, the US military's primary reconnaissance aircraft was the Lockheed U-2. Its main defense wasn't speed or exceptional weaponry, but rather flying above the range of Soviet air defenses. By cruising at 70,000 ft, this slow spy plane was intended to be untouchable. Except, the USSR immediately detected the U-2's overflight missions, and five years after entering service, a surface-to-air missile shot down a U-2 in 1960.
Even before the U-2 was shot down, the United States had already begun exploring concepts for a successor. Several designs were submitted before the CIA selected Lockheed's proposal for a single-seat, high-altitude, Mach 3-capable reconnaissance aircraft. Lockheed's primary competitor was Convair, whose proposals were initially favored for their smaller radar cross-section. However, Lockheed's design proved to be more capable as well as more cost-effective.
| Lockheed A-12/SR-71 variants | Crew | Number produced |  
| --- | --- | --- |  
| Lockheed A-12 Oxcart | One | 13 |  
| Lockheed M-21 | Two | Two |  
| Lockheed YF-12 | Two | Three |  
| Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird | Two | 32 |  
| Total |  | 50 |
The proposal for the CIA would later be designated as the A-12 Oxcart. 13 were produced, along with two M-21s that could deploy drones and three YF-12 interceptor aircraft. The two-seat SR-71 Blackbird was developed for the United States Air Force, and it was the famous variant that served the USAF for decades. In contrast, the A-12 variants for the CIA were retired just a few years after being introduced. In total, 32 SR-71 Blackbirds were built, and the type served the USAF until 1998.

## The Design Of The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird
Credit:Photo:Andy Sutherland I Shutterstock
The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird is one of the most unique-looking aircraft ever made. The Blackbird name comes from its distinctive paint job, as this color was deemed most effective at radiating surface heat, thereby reducing thermal stress on the airframe. The frame itself is shaped to have as small a radar cross-section as was possible in the 1960s, and can be considered an early implementation of stealth technology later seen on planes like the F-117 or B-2 Spirit.
The SR-71 is powered by the same Pratt & Whitney J58 turbojets that powered the A-12. From ground operations to Mach 2, the J58s functioned like conventional after-burning turbojets, producing 32,000 lbs of thrust. Above Mach 2, much of the intake air was bypassed directly into the afterburner, functioning more similarly to a ramjet engine. This has led many to describe it as a hybrid of a turbojet and a ramjet engine.
The SR-71 was designed with tandem cockpits to accommodate a pilot and a systems officer operating the aircraft's surveillance systems. At Mach 3.2, the heat generated by the aircraft would be hot enough to soften aluminum, so Lockheed instead constructed the aircraft out of titanium. This was used for the majority of the SR-71's structure, with the remaining constructed out of polymer composites.

## The SR-71 Blackbird In Service
32 SR-71s were constructed in the 1960s. These were developed in secret by Lockheed's Skunk Works division, and the SR-71 entered service in 1966, nearly 60 years ago. While the SR-71's basic design was derived from the A-12, the SR-71 was larger to accommodate more fuel and a second crew member. The SR-71 also had a longer range than the A-12, and whereas all A-12s were retired in the 1960s, the SR-71 lived on until the late 1990s.
Not willing to risk the political implications of another shootdown, the United States never publicly deployed the SR-71 over Soviet airspace. Instead, the SR-71 skimmed across the borders of the Soviet Union or overflew other nations, such as Vietnam or North Korea. Throughout the Vietnam War, hundreds of North Vietnamese surface-to-air missiles were fired at the SR-71, none of which successfully hit the jet.
The SR-71 was initially retired in 1989, owing to concerns over its operating costs and relevance. In the 1990s, growing concerns over tensions in the Middle East and North Korea led the United States Air Force to reactivate the Blackbirds in 1995. This was short-lived, as the USAF retired the SR-71 once again in 1998. NASA also operated the SR-71 as a research vehicle and retired its final example in 1999.

## The Issues With The SR-71s
Credit:Photo:Philip Arno Photography I Shutterstock
While no SR-71 was ever shot down in combat, 12 were lost in accidents. In 1966, an SR-71 disintegrated in midair at 79,000 ft, resulting in the death of one of its pilots. Additionally, the SR-71 experienced frequent mechanical issues that often required expensive repairs. Of course, this was inevitable given the complex nature of the world's fastest jet, especially considering that it was designed in the 1960s.
On average, an SR-71 could be deployed once per week due to the extensive turnaround times required. Oftentimes, planes would return with missing rivets or damaged components. It was not uncommon for an aircraft to be taken out of service for a month due to the repairs required. Not only did this make the plane impractical, but it also made it impossibly expensive to operate.
Part of why the SR-71 was retired was that its role was succeeded by drones and satellites. These were cheaper to operate, while also possessing far more advanced surveillance technology. Additionally, unlike retrofitted Lockheed U-2s, the SR-71 could not transmit data in real time, meaning that all data could only be retrieved once the aircraft landed. The reactivated SR-71s in the 1990s were upgraded to transmit data in near-real time, but this still proved to be a drawback of the aircraft.

The proposal for the CIA would later be designated as the A-12 Oxcart. 13 were produced, along with two M-21s that could deploy drones and three YF-12 interceptor aircraft. The two-seat SR-71 Blackbird was developed for the United States Air Force, and it was the famous variant that served the USAF for decades. In contrast, the A-12 variants for the CIA were retired just a few years after being introduced. In total, 32 SR-71 Blackbirds were built, and the type served the USAF until 1998.
texts.3:
## The Design Of The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird
Credit:Photo:Andy Sutherland I Shutterstock
The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird is one of the most unique-looking aircraft ever made. The Blackbird name comes from its distinctive paint job, as this color was deemed most effective at radiating surface heat, thereby reducing thermal stress on the airframe. The frame itself is shaped to have as small a radar cross-section as was possible in the 1960s, and can be considered an early implementation of stealth technology later seen on planes like the F-117 or B-2 Spirit.
The SR-71 is powered by the same Pratt & Whitney J58 turbojets that powered the A-12. From ground operations to Mach 2, the J58s functioned like conventional after-burning turbojets, producing 32,000 lbs of thrust. Above Mach 2, much of the intake air was bypassed directly into the afterburner, functioning more similarly to a ramjet engine. This has led many to describe it as a hybrid of a turbojet and a ramjet engine.
The SR-71 was designed with tandem cockpits to accommodate a pilot and a systems officer operating the aircraft's surveillance systems. At Mach 3.2, the heat generated by the aircraft would be hot enough to soften aluminum, so Lockheed instead constructed the aircraft out of titanium. This was used for the majority of the SR-71's structure, with the remaining constructed out of polymer composites.
texts.4:
## The SR-71 Blackbird In Service
32 SR-71s were constructed in the 1960s. These were developed in secret by Lockheed's Skunk Works division, and the SR-71 entered service in 1966, nearly 60 years ago. While the SR-71's basic design was derived from the A-12, the SR-71 was larger to accommodate more fuel and a second crew member. The SR-71 also had a longer range than the A-12, and whereas all A-12s were retired in the 1960s, the SR-71 lived on until the late 1990s.
Not willing to risk the political implications of another shootdown, the United States never publicly deployed the SR-71 over Soviet airspace. Instead, the SR-71 skimmed across the borders of the Soviet Union or overflew other nations, such as Vietnam or North Korea. Throughout the Vietnam War, hundreds of North Vietnamese surface-to-air missiles were fired at the SR-71, none of which successfully hit the jet.
The SR-71 was initially retired in 1989, owing to concerns over its operating costs and relevance. In the 1990s, growing concerns over tensions in the Middle East and North Korea led the United States Air Force to reactivate the Blackbirds in 1995. This was short-lived, as the USAF retired the SR-71 once again in 1998. NASA also operated the SR-71 as a research vehicle and retired its final example in 1999.
texts.5:
## The Issues With The SR-71s
Credit:Photo:Philip Arno Photography I Shutterstock
While no SR-71 was ever shot down in combat, 12 were lost in accidents. In 1966, an SR-71 disintegrated in midair at 79,000 ft, resulting in the death of one of its pilots. Additionally, the SR-71 experienced frequent mechanical issues that often required expensive repairs. Of course, this was inevitable given the complex nature of the world's fastest jet, especially considering that it was designed in the 1960s.
On average, an SR-71 could be deployed once per week due to the extensive turnaround times required. Oftentimes, planes would return with missing rivets or damaged components. It was not uncommon for an aircraft to be taken out of service for a month due to the repairs required. Not only did this make the plane impractical, but it also made it impossibly expensive to operate.
Part of why the SR-71 was retired was that its role was succeeded by drones and satellites. These were cheaper to operate, while also possessing far more advanced surveillance technology. Additionally, unlike retrofitted Lockheed U-2s, the SR-71 could not transmit data in real time, meaning that all data could only be retrieved once the aircraft landed. The reactivated SR-71s in the 1990s were upgraded to transmit data in near-real time, but this still proved to be a drawback of the aircraft.

The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird was a two-seat twin-engine long-range supersonic strategic reconnaissance aircraft produced by Lockheed Corporation. The SR-71 was capable of flying at speeds over Mach 3.2 and at a height of 85,000 feet (25,900 Meter). The SR-71 was in duty from 1964 until 1989 and during a reactivation from 1993 until 1998. It was designed by the Lockheed Advanced Development Projects Devision aka the Lockheed Skunk Works.

The Blackbirds still hold many speed, altitude and distance records for a manned aircraft.
